nodes.label: Migrations as an Explicit Release Step
nodes.rationale: Never run migrations automatically on container boot: two containers starting together both running migrations is a bad afternoon. Seeding is for development; in production the first administrator is created by hand, once.
nodes.norm_label: migrations as an explicit release step

nodes.label: R10 — The Payload Identifies, Never Authorises
nodes.rationale: Resolving an identity payload returns who the member is and what they are entitled to, and performs no state change. This is the whole basis on which a static printed code later became acceptable: possession of the payload alone is worth nothing.
nodes.norm_label: r10 — the payload identifies, never authorises

nodes.label: R11 — No Member Enumeration for Outlet Staff
nodes.rationale: Not filtered — absent. There is no list, search or enumeration endpoint available to the role at all, and the client contains no such call in its API module, so the button does not exist to be found. Adding a member search endpoint for staff convenience is explicitly named as a trap.
nodes.norm_label: r11 — no member enumeration for outlet staff

nodes.label: R3 — Sequential Public Numbers, Opaque Internal Reference
nodes.rationale: Membership numbers are sequential and public (PG-0003) while the internal member reference is an opaque random ID. Because the public number is sequential and printed on cards, anything derived from it is guessable — which is why claim codes and identity payloads both use the opaque id instead.
nodes.norm_label: r3 — sequential public numbers, opaque internal reference

nodes.label: Rotating-QR Digital Card (Archived)
nodes.rationale: An opaque member identifier with a signed, rotating timestamp. Rotation mattered more than usual because 40% off spa treatments and 30% off room rates are worth real money: a static code that could be screenshotted and forwarded would be worth money, so the payload refreshes and an old screenshot fails validation.

nodes.label: Three-Role Staff Access Table (Archived)
nodes.rationale: Administrator (everything), Manager (members and reports, no benefit or staff configuration), Outlet staff (verification page only, no member list or reports). Outlet staff cannot browse the membership, and given who the members are that restriction is not a formality.

nodes.label: Staff Verification Page (Archived)
nodes.rationale: Deliberately a web page rather than a separate application: staff open a URL on any device already behind the counter, sign in with their own account, and use it — no installation, no device procurement, no app store. Part of the dashboard, not a fourth product. Deleted on 2026-08-08.

nodes.label: Q1 — What the QR Code Does
nodes.rationale: Answered three times. Confirmed 2026-07-30 that the code identifies the member; reversed 2026-08-08 to no QR at all with a benefit-request flow; re-answered 2026-08-12 with a static code on the back of the printed card, recovered from commit 2f44daf~1 rather than rewritten. The alternative reading — a code displayed at each outlet and scanned by the member — would have made a 40% discount self-declared.
nodes.norm_label: q1 — what the qr code does

nodes.label: Stage 16 — QR Rendering and Camera Scanning
nodes.rationale: react-qr-code for pure SVG rendering at error-correction level M (not H, which adds ~30% more modules and makes each smaller on a phone screen), minimum 240px with a four-module quiet zone on pure white. @zxing/browser for scanning because BarcodeDetector is unavailable in Safari and counter devices are very often iPads.
nodes.norm_label: stage 16 — qr rendering and camera scanning

nodes.label: Card Scan End to End
nodes.rationale: For a guest who never opens the app, which is the whole point of the card back. Entitlements appear filtered to what this outlet can honour. Worth trying: scan then wait ten minutes before recording (refused, the verification session expired) and scan on one outlet screen then record from another (refused, the session is bound to the account that made it).

nodes.label: Rotating Member Identity Payload v1 (Archived)
nodes.rationale: v1.<member_ref>.<issued_at>.<hmac>, where member_ref is an opaque random identifier and never the printed sequential number. The verification page rejects payloads older than a configured window, defeating forwarded screenshots. Identifies only — entitlement is resolved server-side and possession never applies a discount. The window is a tunable setting, not a hardcoded constant: start around 24 hours and adjust on observed verification failures.

nodes.label: Outlet Staff Enumeration Restriction (Archived)
nodes.rationale: Real enforcement rather than a hidden menu item: no list endpoint exists for the role at all; lookup requires an exact membership number or scanned code with no partial matching or name search; the result is bound to a short-lived verification session; lookups are hard rate limited because sequential printed numbers make an unlimited lookup endpoint an enumeration tool; and failed lookups against non-existent numbers are logged and alerted.

nodes.label: Four-Role Access Matrix (Archived)
nodes.rationale: administrator (everything), manager (member list, detail and reports; explicitly cannot edit benefits, manage staff or export), outlet_staff (verification page only), support (single member by exact ID, no listing or browsing). The manager row's 'can reach' column lists screens rather than operations, which is why manager write access remained an inference rather than a stated requirement.

nodes.label: Missing Verification Session Defect
nodes.rationale: Surfaced by the fetch-then-check guard during Stage 7: the redemption endpoint accepted any member id an outlet account sent, whether or not they had ever resolved that member. Now an HMAC over (staffUserId, memberId, issuedAt) issued by resolve and required by record, tested for expiry, wrong member, wrong account and forged signature.

nodes.label: Archived Product Definition v2
nodes.rationale: Superseded on 2026-08-09 by docs/product-definition.md. Retained as design history: manager, support, outlet-staff and verification-page descriptions grant no access and are not current requirements.

nodes.label: Archived Security Specification v2
nodes.rationale: Near-duplicate predecessor of docs/security-implementation.md, superseded on 2026-08-09. The two differ only in the role model, token lifetime table, client storage wording and §7: v2 describes four staff roles, a verification page and a rotating member identity payload; v3 describes administrator-only access and no QR credential.

nodes.label: Benefit Request Replaces the Guest QR
nodes.rationale: Q1 answered: the client did not want a scanned credential. BenefitRequest PENDING -> APPROVED/DECLINED -> FULFILLED, with Benefit.outletKind routing approvals as data rather than a code mapping. A member cannot approve their own request because requests:create is a MEMBER permission and requests:decide a STAFF one. react-qr-code was kept in web-admin for otpauth:// enrollment. Later reversed on 2026-08-12.
nodes.norm_label: benefit request replaces the guest qr

nodes.label: 160-Bit Crockford Base32 Claim Codes
nodes.rationale: The wireframe's PG- ____ - ____ placeholder is roughly 40 bits, guessable at the rate an activation endpoint could be driven. The security document requires at least 128 bits and forbids deriving the code from the membership number. Crockford excludes I, L, O and U and input is normalised for 1/I and 0/O confusions.

nodes.label: Exhaustive Role Matrix, No Wildcard
nodes.rationale: A wildcard for ADMINISTRATOR means every permission added later is granted silently at the moment it is defined rather than when someone decides it should be. Listing all of them makes each grant a deliberate edit, and the matrix test fails if catalogue and expectations drift apart.

nodes.label: Membership Numbers from a PostgreSQL Sequence
nodes.rationale: Computing MAX(memberNumber)+1 in application code races: two administrators creating a member at the same moment both read the same maximum. member_number_seq plus next_member_number() returning PG-0004 makes that impossible and keeps the format in one place.
nodes.norm_label: membership numbers from a postgresql sequence

nodes.label: Static QR on the Printed Card, Q1 Reversed
nodes.rationale: A printed payload has one timestamp for the life of the card, so a freshness window either rejects the card on day two or is not a freshness window. v2.<member_ref>.<hmac> is static and says so in the version prefix; v1 remains implemented so rotation can be reinstated without reprinting. Acceptable only because the code identifies and grants nothing (R10) — no stronger than the membership number already printed on the front. Derived from the opaque internal id, never the sequential PG- number.
nodes.norm_label: static qr on the printed card, q1 reversed

nodes.label: The Verification Page Is Deleted
nodes.rationale: No counter application: an administrator records every redemption from the dashboard. Recording moved to POST /admin/redemptions with a required outletId, because an administrator at a desk cannot have the outlet inferred and a redemption attributed to the wrong outlet is worse than one attributed to none. The verification session went with it — a genuine reduction in control, acceptable only because every role that can now record already holds members:read.

nodes.label: Camera Requires a Secure Context
nodes.rationale: getUserMedia refuses outside a secure context, so the outlet camera does not work over plain HTTP at all and there is no configuration that changes it. localhost counts and a LAN address does not, which makes TLS a prerequisite for testing a scan on a real counter tablet. Typing a membership number is the documented fallback.

nodes.label: Hero Header Image Placeholder (Lobby / Evening)
nodes.source_location: top band, dashed rectangle x 11.6-280.4, y 12.1-183.6
nodes.rationale: Dashed-outline rectangle labelled 'IMAGE PLACEHOLDER' with the art direction brief 'LOBBY - EVENING' typeset inside it. The hero photograph is unresolved in the design; the slot and its brief are specified while the asset is pending. Repeats identically across A5, A6 and A7, so the header is a shared component rather than per-screen art.

nodes.label: Have an Invitation Code? Entry Point
nodes.source_location: below the credential card, gold text link with caret
nodes.rationale: Secondary route out of sign-in into first-time activation. Rendered as a low-emphasis gold text link with a caret, deliberately outside the credential card, so enrolment never competes visually with the returning-user path. Its presence on the sign-in screen means sign-in is treated as the default surface and activation as the exception.
nodes.norm_label: have an invitation code? entry point

nodes.label: Mobile Number Field (+974)
nodes.source_location: credential card, split input with country-code gutter
nodes.rationale: Split control: fixed '+974' Qatar dial-code segment divided by a hairline rule from the editable local number ('3312 3456' shown as sample data). The dial code is pinned rather than a picker because the property is single-market (Doha), which removes a country selector from the critical path. This is the only credential collected - there is no email or password field anywhere on the screen.

nodes.label: Privilege Guest Programme Eyebrow
nodes.source_location: base of the hero header band, gold letterspaced caps
nodes.rationale: Gold letterspaced 'PRIVILEGE GUEST' caps sit beneath the hotel lockup, naming the loyalty programme as a sub-brand of the property rather than a separate brand. Same treatment repeats on A6; on A7 the slot is taken by the 'ACTIVATE MEMBERSHIP' eyebrow, so the position acts as a per-screen context label.

nodes.label: Send Passcode Action
nodes.source_location: credential card, primary gold pill below the number field
nodes.rationale: Primary CTA. Labelled by its effect ('Send passcode') rather than a generic 'Continue', so the user is told a one-time code is about to arrive by SMS before they leave the screen. Triggers the transition to the A6 passcode screen.

nodes.label: Terms and Privacy Consent Notice
nodes.rationale: 'By continuing you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.' Implicit consent bound to the CTA rather than an explicit checkbox, which keeps the form to a single field but ties acceptance to the act of requesting a passcode.

nodes.label: Change Number Link
nodes.source_location: below the credential card, gold text link
nodes.rationale: Correction path back to A5 for a mistyped number, occupying the same slot below the card that 'Have an invitation code?' occupies on A5 - the position is reserved for the screen's secondary escape route.

nodes.label: Resend Code Countdown
nodes.source_location: between the OTP boxes and the Verify pill
nodes.rationale: 'Resend code in 0:42' - a disabled-until-expiry countdown rather than an always-live resend link. Rate-limits SMS re-sends and sets the expectation that waiting is normal, while promising the action will become available.

nodes.label: Six-Digit OTP Input
nodes.source_location: credential card, six segmented boxes in a row
nodes.rationale: Six discrete rounded boxes rather than one text field. Design state shown mid-entry: '4', '0', '2' filled, box four holding the caret and outlined in gold as the focus ring, boxes five and six showing dot placeholders. Segmenting the code makes length legible at a glance and gives per-digit focus feedback.

nodes.label: Verify Action
nodes.rationale: Primary CTA in the same gold pill slot the 'Send passcode' button occupies on A5, giving the two-step sign-in a consistent commit position.

nodes.label: Activate Membership Action
nodes.source_location: activation card, primary gold pill at card foot
nodes.rationale: Primary CTA committing code, phone number and channel preferences in a single submission.

nodes.label: Already Activated? Sign In Link
nodes.source_location: below the activation card, gold text link with caret
nodes.rationale: Return route to A5, mirroring the 'Have an invitation code?' link in the opposite direction. The pair makes sign-in and activation mutually reachable so a guest who lands on the wrong surface is never stuck.

nodes.label: Invitation Code Field (PG-XXXX-XXXX)
nodes.source_location: activation card, first field, gold focus outline
nodes.rationale: Masked format hint 'PG-XXXX-XXXX' teaches the code shape before typing; the 'PG' prefix encodes Privilege Guest. Given the gold focus outline as the first and highest-priority field on the screen, while the mobile field below it sits in the neutral resting state - the code is what gates entry.

nodes.label: Enrolment Mobile Number Field
nodes.source_location: activation card, second field with helper text
nodes.rationale: Same split +974 control as A5, annotated with the helper line 'This becomes your sign-in method.' The copy makes the enrolment step explicitly bind the phone number as the permanent identity for all later sign-ins, explaining why no password is ever requested.

nodes.label: Notification Channel Preferences
nodes.source_location: activation card, below hairline rule; Email and SMS toggle rows
nodes.rationale: Two toggles separated from the credential fields by a hairline rule. Email ships on (gold, knob right), SMS ships off (grey, knob left) - marketing consent defaults to the channel the invitation already arrived on, and leaves the transactional SMS channel unclaimed for promotional use. Collected during activation rather than deferred to a settings screen.

nodes.label: A5 Sign-In Screen
nodes.rationale: Returning-member entry surface for the Steigenberger Hotel Doha 'Privilege Guest' app. Headline 'Welcome back' / 'Sign in with your mobile number'. Layout is a three-band phone screen: branded hero header (image placeholder + STEIGENBERGER wordmark + PRIVILEGE GUEST eyebrow), a raised rounded card holding the single credential field and primary CTA, then a secondary text link and a legal footer pinned to the bottom. Dark luxury palette (near-black #2a211d ground, champagne/gold #e8d3a0 accent) with a single filled gold pill as the only primary action, so the screen has exactly one obvious next step.

nodes.label: A6 Passcode Verification Screen
nodes.rationale: Second step of sign-in: one-time passcode challenge. Headline 'Enter your passcode' with the subhead 'We sent a 6-digit code to +974 3312 3456' echoing the exact number entered on A5, so the user can verify the destination without going back. Reuses the A5 header band and card shell verbatim; adds a circular back button at top-left, the first screen in the flow to have one.

nodes.label: A7 Activate Membership Screen
nodes.rationale: First-time enrolment surface, reached from the 'Have an invitation code?' link on A5. Eyebrow 'ACTIVATE MEMBERSHIP', headline 'Welcome, Privilege Guest', subhead 'Use the code from your welcome email'. The header band is compressed (hero ends at y 147 vs 195 on A5/A6) to make room for the tallest card in the set, which stacks invitation code, mobile number, a rule, notification toggles and the commit button. Carries a back button like A6.

nodes.label: Steigenberger Hotel & Residence Doha Lockup
nodes.rationale: Standalone three-tier brand lockup asset, not a screen: serif STEIGENBERGER wordmark over letterspaced 'HOTEL & RESIDENCE' (#C0C5C7 vector paths) over 'DOHA' (#EDEAE4). Built for a dark ground - all fills are light greys and off-whites with no background plate. Newer than the A5-A7 exports and carries the 'HOTEL & RESIDENCE' descriptor where the screens render 'HOTEL DOHA', so it reads as the corrected or canonical lockup for the header slot.

nodes.label: Steigenberger Wordmark Raster Asset (486x242)
nodes.source_location: pattern0_45_4640 / pattern1_45_4640, images image0_45_4640 and image1_45_4640
nodes.rationale: The serif wordmark is not vector - it is a pair of 486x242 embedded PNGs (a luminance mask plus a colour plate, sha1 bddf6d1c0ab9 and 0d96b607b3e3) applied through SVG patterns behind a luminance mask. The identical byte-for-byte pair is embedded in A5, A6 and A7, making it the hard shared dependency that ties the lockup to every auth screen. Shipping the exported raster rather than re-tracing the serif preserves the licensed brand letterforms exactly.

nodes.label: Passwordless Phone-Number Authentication
nodes.rationale: The flow carries no password field, no email field and no 'forgot password' affordance anywhere across A5/A6/A7. Identity is the mobile number and the proof is a transient SMS passcode. Trade-off accepted: guests never manage a credential and there is no reset path to support, at the cost of a hard dependency on SMS deliverability - which is why A6 carries both a resend timer and a call-the-front-desk fallback.

nodes.label: Front Desk Human Fallback
nodes.source_location: footer, replacing the A5 legal notice
nodes.rationale: 'Didn't receive it? Check your SMS filter or call the front desk on 4020 1666.' Terminates the failure branch in staff rather than in software - the hospitality context supplies a human recovery path that a generic consumer app lacks. Occupies the footer slot A5 gives to the legal notice, so the footer is a per-screen support slot. Naming the likely cause (SMS filtering) before the phone number tries self-service first.

nodes.label: Invitation-Only Membership Enrolment
nodes.rationale: There is no open sign-up anywhere in the flow - the only way to become a member is to redeem a PG-prefixed code issued out of band in a welcome email. Membership is a closed, hotel-issued privilege rather than a self-serve account, which is what licenses the 'Welcome, Privilege Guest' greeting before any identity has been verified: the design assumes anyone holding a code is already known to the property.

nodes.label: R16 — Members Are Suspended, Never Deleted
nodes.rationale: DELETE on Member is revoked from the application role. This is also what makes deletion-by-anonymisation the only available shape for a deletion request, since severing the link to redemption history lets aggregate reporting survive.
nodes.norm_label: r16 — members are suspended, never deleted

nodes.label: Monorepo Repository Structure
nodes.rationale: docs/ read-only references, apps/api plus one app per client surface, packages/shared for Zod schemas and types, and PROGRESS.md and DECISIONS.md maintained per stage. The root workspaces globs already cover apps/*, so client apps needed no configuration change when they arrived.

nodes.label: Decided Stack
nodes.rationale: TypeScript strict on Node 20+, Fastify, PostgreSQL 15+, Prisma, Zod, @node-rs/argon2, jose, Vitest + Supertest, React + Vite clients, npm workspaces. Separate React apps rather than one, because they have entirely different authentication and authorization models.

nodes.label: §12 Engineering Checklist
nodes.rationale: Thirty items across credentials, tokens, authorization and data. The checklist Stage 14's security review works through item by item, confirming each with a file reference or recording why it is deferred.

nodes.label: Token Version and Forced Re-Authentication
nodes.rationale: tv on the user record: incrementing it invalidates every outstanding access token — the mechanism behind logout-everywhere, role change and emergency revocation. Triggered by password change, role change, staff offboarding, membership suspension, suspected compromise and user-initiated logout-everywhere.

nodes.label: Access Plus Opaque Refresh Token Architecture
nodes.rationale: A JWT cannot be individually revoked without building the server-side state it was meant to avoid, so the refresh token is opaque, hashed and carries a family ID. Access 10 min (panel) / 30 min (member app); refresh 12 hours (administrator) / 30 days sliding (member). Staff lifetimes are deliberately short: a member's session persisting is a convenience, a staff session persisting on a shared device is an exposure. Algorithm pinned server-side; iss and aud validated, not merely present.
nodes.norm_label: access plus opaque refresh token architecture

nodes.label: Deviations from Spec
nodes.rationale: Exactly two: Member.tokenVersion added beyond the build plan's Stage 1 schema, and HS256 rather than EdDSA/RS256 for access token signing. Both traced to explicit clauses in the security document. Q5 and Q6 are gaps, not silent deviations — both were flagged rather than built around.

nodes.label: Database-Level Redemption Immutability — Confirmed
nodes.rationale: Exercised against a real database: the application connects as pgp_app, which holds only SELECT and INSERT on Redemption. Migrations run as the schema owner through Prisma's directUrl, because an owner cannot be denied its own tables and the revocation would otherwise be theatre.

nodes.label: Archived Build Plan
nodes.rationale: The authoritative build order for Stages 0-14, superseded in part on 2026-08-09. Reference documents are the authoritative source of what to build; this file is the order to build it in.

nodes.label: Technical Decision Log
nodes.rationale: Append-only record of every technical choice the specification did not dictate, each with alternatives considered and the reason. Newest last.

nodes.label: Security Implementation Specification v3
nodes.rationale: Current and authoritative, at engineering level. Overrides convenience, speed and preference; where any document conflicts with it on a security matter, it wins.

nodes.label: Build Progress Log
nodes.rationale: Per-stage record of files created, acceptance criteria met, open questions and deviations. Maintained at the end of every stage before committing, as the build plan requires.

nodes.label: Post-Build Roadmap
nodes.rationale: Continues the build plan's stage numbering and rules, dropping only rule 1 so styling is in scope. Covers what remains after Stage 14: a correct, tested, well-secured engine with no bodywork.

nodes.label: Security Review Against the §12 Checklist
nodes.rationale: Every item in the security specification's checklist with its status and where it is enforced. Nothing is marked confirmed on the strength of code alone: where a test proves it the test is named, and where the proof is a database privilege the privilege was exercised against a real database.

nodes.label: Six Prime Directives
nodes.rationale: 1 logic only, no styling (retired at Stage 17). 2 do not invent features. 3 security rules are not negotiable — where any document conflicts with the security specification on a security matter, it wins. 4 stop and ask rather than guess: implement the documented assumption, add TODO(open-question), record it. 5 one stage at a time. 6 tests are part of the stage.

nodes.label: HS256 Access Tokens Within a Single Deployable
nodes.rationale: The security document prefers EdDSA/RS256 but explicitly permits HS256 within a single deployable. This build is one Fastify process serving all surfaces. Revisit if the API is split, at which point asymmetric signing lets each verifier work without holding the signing secret.
nodes.norm_label: hs256 access tokens within a single deployable

nodes.label: Member.tokenVersion Added Beyond the Build Plan
nodes.rationale: The build plan gives tokenVersion to StaffUser only, but the security document lists membership suspension among the events that must force re-authentication and names token version as the mechanism. Prime directive 3 gives the security document precedence; recorded as a deviation rather than a silent schema change.
nodes.norm_label: member.tokenversion added beyond the build plan

nodes.label: @pgp/shared Resolves to TypeScript Source
nodes.rationale: Pointing exports at ./src/index.ts means tsx, Vitest and tsc --noEmit all resolve the same files with no build ordering between workspaces. Cost: a compiled production build of api will need shared bundled or pre-built.

nodes.label: Suspension Increments tokenVersion and Revokes Refresh Families
nodes.rationale: A status check alone leaves an already-issued access token valid until it expires — up to 30 minutes for a member. Refresh tokens are separate server-side state and are revoked explicitly, or the member could mint a fresh access token seconds later.
nodes.norm_label: suspension increments tokenversion and revokes refresh families

nodes.label: tsx for Development, No Build Step
nodes.rationale: tsx runs the ESM/NodeNext sources directly and watches without an intermediate dist/, keeping the workspace-to-workspace import path honest. No stage's acceptance criteria require a compiled artefact yet.
nodes.norm_label: tsx for development, no build step

nodes.label: Primary Acceptance Journey
nodes.rationale: Twelve steps in order against one running server, no step stubbed, each using what the previous produced — from administrator creating a member through to the headline pair: changing the dining discount to 20% and the member client reflecting it with no restart or deployment.

nodes.label: R7 — Redemptions Are Immutable
nodes.rationale: No UPDATE, no DELETE — a correction is a new reversing row. Enforced at the database level rather than in application code, so neither a bug in a handler nor a compromised API process can talk it out of the guarantee.

nodes.label: Nightly Encrypted Backups and Restore Drill
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL is the authoritative record and the Google Sheet must never be treated as a backup. Immutable redemptions and append-only audit logs protect against tampering and do nothing about a lost disk. An untested backup is not a backup — restore one into a scratch database before launch and again quarterly, with someone other than the script's author following the runbook.
nodes.norm_label: nightly encrypted backups and restore drill

nodes.label: Four-Hostname Caddy Topology
nodes.rationale: my. and api. are public; outlet. and admin. are internal only. Four things run and three are static files. The API is public and has to be — members open the app from home, from a plane, from another country. What is restricted is not the backend but which routes answer which source addresses.

nodes.label: Post-Deploy Verification Checklist
nodes.rationale: Not a checklist to skim — each item has failed silently in a real system. TLS on all four hosts, security headers, internal hosts refusing an outside address, CORS not answering a stranger, liveness and readiness distinguishable, R7 holding, and no member name in container logs.

nodes.label: Database Privilege Backstop
nodes.rationale: Even without competing tenants, defence in depth is worth the small cost: the application role holds no DELETE on members or redemptions and no UPDATE on redemptions. Destructive operations require a separate migration role.

nodes.label: Threat Model
nodes.rationale: Curious or paid-off staff, external attacker after the membership list, opportunistic non-member after 30-40% discounts, dishonest staff recording redemptions that did not occur, and an insider bulk-extracting. Note the ordering: in version 1 the top threat was points fraud; here it is disclosure of who the members are and where they have been.

nodes.label: Stage 21 — Deployment
nodes.rationale: Host in Qatar because the membership list is a record of named, prominent individuals and their movements; in-region hosting removes a whole class of cross-border transfer argument before anyone has it. One VM, Docker Compose, Caddy in front — for a programme whose reference card is number three, orchestration is a liability.

nodes.label: Six Verification Layers
nodes.rationale: Database reachable, schema current, types sound, tests pass, server boots, end to end. A failure at layer n makes the layers above it meaningless. Layer 5 matters on its own: the test suite builds the app in-process, so it can pass while npm run dev fails — startup-only faults like a missing env var, plugin ordering or the R17 boot check surface only there.

nodes.label: Log Redaction — Confirmed
nodes.rationale: Two mechanisms because either alone leaves a gap: pino redact paths for shapes the app logs itself, and a serializer that walks whatever a caller passes at any depth. The second is what makes log.info({ member }) safe — the call nobody anticipates, made while debugging something else. Opaque references pass through, or redaction would strip the identifiers that make an entry useful.

nodes.label: Deployment Procedure
nodes.rationale: The procedure companion to the roadmap's hosting section: written to be followed in order, from localhost to something members and staff actually use.

nodes.label: Managed Postgres Silently Breaks R7
nodes.rationale: Azure Postgres Flexible Server adds $16.06/mo minimum and destroys the redemption-immutability guarantee unless pgp_app / pgp_owner are created by hand. Paying money to break a security property is a bad trade; the container on the same VM is $0.

nodes.label: Shared Caddy api_proxy Snippet with CIDR Restriction Inside
nodes.rationale: Both clients hardcode BASE = '/api' but the production Caddyfile proxied nothing, so every production API call would have returned the HTML document and the apps would have loaded then silently failed. Fixing it opened a hole — proxying /api/* on my.<domain> would expose /api/admin/* publicly — so the CIDR restriction now lives inside the shared snippet, safe to import anywhere rather than safe only where somebody remembered to pair it with a guard.
nodes.norm_label: shared caddy api_proxy snippet with cidr restriction inside

nodes.label: CHECK Constraints for Invariants Prisma Cannot Express
nodes.rationale: minGuests/maxGuests coherence, positive party size, percentages within 0-100, outlet required on OUTLET_STAFF, and a reversal not pointing at itself are cheap in the database and cannot then be bypassed by a bug in a handler. A backstop, not the rule.
nodes.norm_label: check constraints for invariants prisma cannot express

nodes.label: Two Database URLs: App Role and Owner Role
nodes.rationale: A revocation is meaningless if the application connects as the schema owner — an owner cannot be denied its own tables. DATABASE_URL is the least-privileged pgp_app role; DATABASE_MIGRATION_URL is pgp_owner, reached through Prisma's directUrl so no wrapper script is needed.
nodes.norm_label: two database urls: app role and owner role

nodes.label: Split Liveness and Readiness Probes
nodes.rationale: Folding the database check into GET /health makes the probe unable to distinguish a dead process from a dead database, and makes npm test require a live database. GET /health/ready runs SELECT 1 instead. Prisma connects lazily so /health can still answer during an outage.

nodes.label: INTERNAL_CIDR Staff Network Restriction
nodes.rationale: Must contain the staff/back-of-house VLAN and the VPN, never guest Wi-Fi merely because it is inside the building. A tablet on cellular is refused by design. /admin/* must be restricted on the public API host as well as the dashboard hostname, or the restriction is decorative. Defence in depth: source address reduces exposure and never becomes identity.

nodes.label: pgp_app / pgp_owner Role Separation
nodes.rationale: docker/postgres/init/01-app-role.sh only runs on first initialisation of an empty data directory. Point the API at a managed Postgres, connect as the owner because that is what the connection string came with, and redemption immutability disappears silently — no test fails, no error appears. A raw UPDATE smoke test must be run after every deploy that touches the database.

nodes.label: Confidentiality of the Membership List
nodes.rationale: The reference card is issued to a member of the Qatari ruling family. A membership list of this kind is a record of named, prominent individuals and their movements — when they dined, when they visited the spa, how often they stay. That is not ordinary customer data, and a leak would be serious independent of any regulatory penalty. Every access-control decision in the build follows from this.

nodes.label: Three Audiences, One API Process
nodes.rationale: The instinct to put the backend on an intranet cannot work: every member screen is an API call and an API reachable only from hotel wifi is an app that only works while standing in the lobby. What can be restricted is which routes are reachable from where, done at the reverse proxy by hostname and source address. The database is never published, on any address.

nodes.label: Three Ordering Constraints
nodes.rationale: Stage 15 before 16 (a different Q1 answer wastes the scanner work); Stage 16 before 19 (MFA enrollment needs the QR renderer); Stage 21 partly before finishing 16 (camera access needs a secure context, so deploy early and unfinished rather than late and complete). Stage 17 is the one genuinely parallelisable split.

nodes.label: Known Failure Modes
nodes.rationale: Every one has actually happened here: PowerShell execution policy, .env not loading outside apps/api, npm swallowing a leading -- before a script flag, EPERM renaming the Prisma engine DLL while the API holds it, a UTF-8 BOM from Out-File breaking a migration, non-ASCII characters killing a .ps1, PowerShell mangling case-sensitive table quoting, and suite-only failures from shared in-memory state.

nodes.label: Idempotency Key Lookup Scoped to the Caller's Outlet
nodes.rationale: The key is client-supplied, so an unscoped lookup would let a guessed key disclose another outlet's redemption — member id, benefit, party size, bill amount. The same key with different content returns 409 rather than silently returning the original, because that would hide a client bug.
nodes.norm_label: idempotency key lookup scoped to the caller's outlet

nodes.label: Fetch-Then-Check Enforced by Source Scanning
nodes.rationale: It is a property of how handlers are written, not something a running server can be asked about. fetch-then-check.test.ts scans src/routes for Prisma reads of scoped models and requires a scope fragment in the same statement, with an exempt list carrying written reasons. The guard resolves a where passed as a variable within a 25-line lookbehind.

nodes.label: R13 — Cohorts Below Five Are Suppressed
nodes.rationale: With a membership of dozens, a report filtered to one benefit, one outlet and one week may describe exactly one person. Without suppression, aggregate reporting becomes an indirect route to individual member movements.
nodes.norm_label: r13 — cohorts below five are suppressed

nodes.label: Google Sheets Mirror Deployment Prerequisites
nodes.rationale: Leave GOOGLE_SHEETS_SYNC_ENABLED=false until the hotel approves Workspace and data residency, a dedicated workbook exists with link sharing off, named administrators are Viewers and only the service account is Editor, and the private key is in the deployment secret store. Perform one manual reconciliation and confirm no member name, phone or email appears before enabling the schedule.

nodes.label: Minimum Cohort Size of Five
nodes.rationale: The one threshold the specification states outright. Below it the endpoint returns 'insufficient data' rather than a number, because otherwise aggregate reporting becomes an indirect route to individual member movements — precisely what the document exists to protect.

nodes.label: Server-Side Metric and Dimension Allowlist
nodes.rationale: No client-supplied SQL ever, including fragments. Metrics and dimensions come from a server-side map of identifiers to validated expressions, and anything absent from the map is rejected before a query is built. Exports are a separate permission: administrator-only, rate-limited, individually audited and alerted.

nodes.label: Stage 26 — Hotel-Facing Google Sheets Mirror
nodes.rationale: Five managed tabs — _Sync, Members, Benefits, Outlets, Redemptions — rebuilt in full every five minutes. Requests are deliberately absent in v1 because free-text notes and live state do not belong in a standing bulk export. Code acceptance is complete; operational acceptance (hotel approval, data residency, workbook sharing, secret storage) is not.

nodes.label: Small-Cohort Suppression — Confirmed
nodes.rationale: The cohort is distinct members, not rows: four redemptions by one member is a cohort of one, and it is the member the report must not identify. The cohort size is withheld along with the figures, since '3 members' is the same disclosure stated outright.

nodes.label: Google Sheets Mirror as a Conditional External Surface
nodes.rationale: Code controls confirmed; production activation not yet approved. Enabling it creates a standing bulk export outside Fastify RBAC, so the hotel must first approve Workspace and its data residency, disable link sharing, restrict named humans to Viewer, grant Editor only to the service identity, and store and rotate its key through the deployment secret manager.
nodes.norm_label: google sheets mirror as a conditional external surface

nodes.label: Admin Overview Screen and Measured Charts
nodes.rationale: The dashboard opened on a hundred-row member table while the headline figures sat behind a tab. Benefit names are nominal so every bar wears one hue and there is no legend; reach is a meter not a doughnut. Colours were chosen by measuring contrast — --c-primary-soft measures 1.13:1 on white and is unusable as a meter track. Two silent defects found: the insufficient_data sentinel rendering into a KPI tile, and report rows mistyped as MemberRow.
nodes.norm_label: admin overview screen and measured charts

nodes.label: CSV Export with BOM and Unconditional Quoting
nodes.rationale: The export returned JSON that finance — the one audience it exists for — could not open. Now text/csv with a Content-Disposition filename carrying discount_pct (the rate applied on that visit) and a computed discount_value. Quoting is unconditional because an outlet called 'Crust, Doha' would shift every column after it, and Excel reads a UTF-8 file without a BOM as the local codepage.
nodes.norm_label: csv export with bom and unconditional quoting

nodes.label: Google Sheets as a Sanitised One-Way Mirror
nodes.rationale: Replacing PostgreSQL was rejected: the programme depends on transactions, uniqueness, idempotency, immutable redemptions and security records Sheets cannot enforce. A repeatable-read full snapshot publishes every five minutes outside all request handlers, so Google latency cannot fail a member creation. Treated as a standing bulk export, so the existing export policy holds: membership numbers may leave, names/phones/emails may not.
nodes.norm_label: google sheets as a sanitised one-way mirror

nodes.label: Discount Rate Recorded on the Redemption
nodes.rationale: Reading the rate back from the Benefit put R14 (editable percentages) in silent conflict with reporting: moving dining from 25% to 20% restated every month already reported, and a member's own history contradicted their receipt. discountPctApplied and benefitVersion are NOT NULL with no default, so every creation site must state a rate. A reversal copies the original's rate rather than re-reading the benefit.
nodes.norm_label: discount rate recorded on the redemption

nodes.label: Outlet Device Token Provisioning
nodes.rationale: Admin -> Outlets issues one token per physical device; the API stores only its SHA-256 digest so the plaintext cannot be retrieved later. Rotate when a token may have been copied, revoke one-way when a device is lost. Never share one outlet-wide token: separate rows are what let a lost tablet be disabled without taking the other counters offline. Device labels become the outlet-level actor on immutable redemption history.

nodes.label: Administrator Panel
nodes.rationale: Members, redemptions with export, reporting, and benefit management. The programme currently produces no data at all, so even simple counts are a significant improvement. Test of success: changing the F&B discount from 25% to 20% is a form field, not a code change.

nodes.label: Administrator as the Only Hotel-Facing Account Type
nodes.rationale: No manager, support or outlet-staff logins and no reduced staff panel. Historical database role values may remain solely to preserve attribution on old records; they grant no access and are not shown in the product.
nodes.norm_label: administrator as the only hotel-facing account type

nodes.label: Logging Redaction and Append-Only Audit
nodes.rationale: Application logs contain no member names, phone numbers or email addresses — log the opaque reference only, enforced by a redaction layer on the logger rather than by convention. The audit log is separate, append-only and restricted, covering every record viewed, every lookup, export, benefit change, membership change, authentication event and authorization denial. Who viewed which member's history is itself sensitive information.

nodes.label: Outlet Fulfilment Delivery Summary
nodes.rationale: Two client requests built together because the second is only useful once the first exists: a request stops being a petition, and outlets get their own screen at apps/web-outlet. Also cleared two pre-existing blockers — a publisher.ts narrowing gap that broke the production image build, and the test suite inheriting OTP_DELIVERY_CHANNEL from a developer's .env.

nodes.label: Stage 27 — Administrator-Only Hotel Access
nodes.rationale: Client-confirmed correction: keep the member guest app and administrator panel, retire every other staff role and surface. Migration 20260809210000_administrator_only_accounts suspends legacy rows and revokes their sessions without deleting or relabelling historical redemption attribution.

nodes.label: Stage 28 — Outlet Fulfilment
nodes.rationale: Partly reverses Stage 27: apps/web-outlet exists, so there are three applications again, though ADMINISTRATOR remains the only account a named person holds. Did not do: the camera on real counter hardware (needs TLS), and a printable card back — the largest remaining gap in the feature as the client described it.

nodes.label: Managing Outlet Devices
nodes.rationale: One row per physical device, not one shared token per outlet. Copy the plaintext from the one-time panel immediately — the API stores only a SHA-256 digest. Rotation and revocation increment tokenVersion and revoke the refresh family so an open session dies rather than lasting out its access token. A blank Last used means provisioned but never signed in.

nodes.label: Request Flow End to End
nodes.rationale: Nobody approves anything: a guest is entitled to every published benefit the moment they join, so a request is a notice telling one outlet to expect them. Three rules worth exercising — announce twice in a minute (429, and still refused after an API restart because the throttle counts rows), confirm the same notice twice (already_closed), and look for another outlet's notice (404, not 403).

nodes.label: Append-Only Audit Log — Confirmed
nodes.rationale: UPDATE and DELETE on AuditLog are revoked from the application role, so a caller cannot rewrite its own trail. Entries carry the membership number, never the name, and a failed login does not record the attempted email — that would write attacker-chosen strings, and occasionally a real address typed into the wrong box, into the trail.

nodes.label: Per-Device Outlet Authentication Addendum
nodes.rationale: The current authority wherever older verification-page or Google-default text conflicts. An outlet holds exactly outlet:queue, outlet:fulfil and outlet:resolve and notably not redemptions:record, because that route takes the outlet from the request body — holding it would be a way to record against another outlet's room. The exchange endpoint hashes malformed and truncated values through the same indexed lookup and uniform 401 path as unknown credentials.

nodes.label: One Hotel-Facing Account Type: Administrator
nodes.rationale: Client confirmed the required product is the member guest app plus the administrator panel. The role selector is removed rather than hidden and the server sets the role instead of trusting a request field. Legacy rows are suspended rather than converted, because converting them would turn a later reinstatement into privilege escalation.

nodes.label: In-Memory Two-Dimensional Rate Limiter
nodes.rationale: Limiting per IP and per identifier at once on the same route is not directly expressible with a single off-the-shelf plugin instance. A ~40-line fixed-window module was simpler to get exactly right. Known limitation: limits reset on restart and are not shared across processes.

nodes.label: Outlet Authentication Is Device-Token-Only
nodes.rationale: An outlet account means the labelled counter device, not a mailbox. No Google button, OAuth callback, password login, allowlist or secondary path. Outlet.notifyEmail has exactly one job — notifications — and is not copied into StaffUser or used to recover a token. Local login is deliberately the production login: the development session-bundle helper is removed so a JWT bundle cannot be mistaken for the standing credential.

nodes.label: Outlet Accounts Authenticating Through Google
nodes.rationale: Real OAuth with the ID token verified against Google's published keys — issuer, audience, nonce and email_verified all checked. Google authenticates, the application authorizes: both the hosted-domain gate and an active OUTLET_STAFF row must pass. Cannot enforce whether the account's own 2FA is switched on, which Google does not disclose. Superseded by per-device tokens later the same day.

nodes.label: Per-Device Outlet Tokens
nodes.rationale: Google's operational dependencies (OAuth client, Workspace mailboxes, shared-account 2FA policy) cannot be completed by deploying this application. pgo_ tokens carry 256 bits of entropy, are stored only as a unique SHA-256 digest, and are accepted only by POST /outlet/auth/token. One token per physical device makes the blast radius the device's one outlet. Explicitly one factor, accepted for the pilot.

nodes.label: The Benefit Request Becomes a Notice
nodes.rationale: BenefitRequest is the guest announcing themselves; Redemption is the immutable record a discount was given. Removing the administrator in the middle leaves SENT -> FULFILLED with NOT_USED as the other ending. Creating requests as APPROVED was rejected as a smaller diff that would put the word 'approved' in the audit log for something nobody approved. The one-per-minute throttle counts rows on requestedAt so a deploy does not hand anybody a fresh allowance.
nodes.norm_label: the benefit request becomes a notice

nodes.label: WhatsApp Considered and Rejected
nodes.rationale: Automatic WhatsApp means Meta's Cloud API: verified business account, dedicated number, pre-approved templates and a per-message fee; the free wa.me link needs a human to press it. The destination is the outlet's own screen instead. One deliberate departure from the redaction policy: an outlet notice carries the membership number and benefit because it is useless without them — a difference of audience, and the guest's name is still never sent.

nodes.label: TRUST_PROXY Behind Caddy
nodes.rationale: Fastify sees the proxy's address unless told to read X-Forwarded-For. Leave it off and every per-IP rate-limit bucket collapses into one and every audited ipAddress records the proxy — both controls silently stop working while appearing present. Off by default, because a directly-exposed API must not believe the header or a caller picks their own bucket and forges their own audit trail.

nodes.label: Member Phone Plus One-Time Passcode
nodes.rationale: No passwords for members. Codes from a cryptographically secure source, stored hashed because a leaked table of live codes is account takeover, 5-minute TTL, single use, constant-time comparison, maximum 5 attempts, rate limited per number, per IP and globally to prevent SMS-pumping fraud.

nodes.label: OTP Codes Hashed with HMAC-SHA256
nodes.rationale: A 6-digit OTP is a ~20-bit space, trivially brute-forced offline at any hash speed, so a slow hash buys nothing. The real defenses are the 5-minute TTL and 5-attempt lockout. HMAC keyed by OTP_CODE_HMAC_SECRET still prevents rainbow-table matching against a leaked table.

nodes.label: Uniform Responses and Timings
nodes.rationale: Login, activation and reset return identical responses and comparable timings whether or not the identifier exists. On a membership this exclusive, confirming that a given phone number belongs to a member is itself a disclosure.

nodes.label: AWS me-central-1 / me-south-1 Alternative
nodes.rationale: AWS operates no Qatar region; the nearest are UAE and Bahrain. Costs the same on demand and gives up the in-country argument. Reserved pricing ($18.76 vs Azure's estimated $27) is the one genuine advantage, worth about $8/month.

nodes.label: Azure Qatar Central Hosting
nodes.rationale: Standard_B2als_v2 (2 vCPU / 4 GiB) at $31.32/mo plus a 64 GiB Standard SSD E6 at $5.76 and ~$2 backup blob, giving ~$39/mo on demand. Matches DEPLOYMENT.md §2's spec exactly.

nodes.label: Cost-Gated Launch Sequence
nodes.rationale: The slow items are administrative, not technical: D-U-N-S lookup, Play organisation account and the DPIA all start now because they have lead times and cost nothing. Managed Postgres, managed containers, Wallet passes and React Native are explicitly deferred.

nodes.label: App Store Fees, $124 Year One
nodes.rationale: Google Play $25 once plus Apple $99/year. Commission is $0 because nothing is sold in-app — benefits are redeemed in person. The real cost is engineering time (Capacitor, weeks) and calendar time (D-U-N-S issuance, organisation verification, Apple review).

nodes.label: Three-Phase Budget
nodes.rationale: Pilot ~$42/mo (one outlet, ten members, four weeks); public PWA launch ~$140-155/mo all-SMS or ~$50-75/mo email-first; both stores ~$150-165/mo recurring. Year one all in, excluding legal and engineering: roughly $1,900-3,200.

nodes.label: Twilio Qatar SMS Pricing
nodes.rationale: $0.2634 per outbound segment to Qatari numbers, plus $1.15/mo long-code lease. Arabic bodies use UCS-2 and halve the 160-character segment budget to 70, silently doubling the bill.

nodes.label: Unpriced DPIA and Privacy Policy
nodes.rationale: Deliberately given no number because regional legal fees are not published anywhere linkable. Likely the largest single one-off line, and it gates both store submissions since both stores require a privacy policy at a public URL. Governed by Qatar's Law No. 13 of 2016, supervised by the NCSA.

nodes.label: The Three Unsourced Figures
nodes.rationale: Azure 1-year reserved instance (~$27/mo, not on the public retail API), legal/DPIA (no published rates), and engineering time. Stated plainly so they are not mistaken for quoted prices.

nodes.label: Data Protection Obligations
nodes.rationale: Consent captured per channel, unticked by default, stored with timestamp and wording version, withdrawable with immediate effect. Deletion honoured by irreversible anonymisation rather than row removal so aggregate reporting survives. A DPIA is required before launch. Hosting region decided before infrastructure is built. No special-category data: spa treatment records can imply health information, so record that a spa benefit was used, not what treatment was taken.

nodes.label: Stage 24 — Pre-Launch, Non-Engineering
nodes.rationale: DPIA, privacy policy and terms content, consent wording version 1, staff training, a data retention policy that has no answer in code yet, a restore drill run by someone other than the author, and a narrow pilot — one outlet, ten members, four weeks.

nodes.label: Deferred — Data Protection Impact Assessment
nodes.rationale: Explicitly not an engineering task. Failing to carry one out carries an administrative fine of up to QAR 1,000,000 on its own, independent of any breach, and the hosting region must be settled before infrastructure is built given restrictions on transferring personal data outside Qatar. Blocking for launch rather than for development.

nodes.label: Google Play Organisation Account Exemption
nodes.rationale: Google's 12-tester closed-test rule is scoped to personal accounts created after 13 Nov 2023. The organisation exemption follows from that scoping but is not published as a guarantee — confirm with Play support in writing before planning a launch date around it.

nodes.label: In-Region Qatar Hosting Is Free
nodes.rationale: Azure Qatar Central at $31.32/mo versus AWS UAE at $29.78/mo is a $1.54 difference, so the assumed in-region premium does not exist. Moving to AWS to save money gives up the data-residency argument for nothing.

nodes.label: SMS Is the Only Steeply Scaling Cost
nodes.rationale: Past roughly 120 members, one-time passcodes cost more per month than the entire server; at 1,000 members it is eight times the server. Hosting is flat, SMS is linear, and the passcode-channel decision is worth more than every other cost choice combined.
nodes.norm_label: sms is the only steeply scaling cost

nodes.label: Quoted vs Derived Sourcing Discipline
nodes.rationale: Every figure is labelled quoted (linked to a vendor page or API response) or derived (arithmetic shown, inputs linked). Assumptions are stated next to the figures that rest on them, so no number can be mistaken for a vendor price.

nodes.label: Member Guest App
nodes.rationale: Four sections: Explore, Offers, Search, Profile. Nothing is hidden behind another tap because the printed sheet it replaces showed everything at once. Redemption history matters more than it appears — it answers 'did I already use the spa discount this month' without a phone call.

nodes.label: Invitation-Only Onboarding and Claim Flow
nodes.rationale: Runs in the opposite direction from a normal app: administrator creates the record and issues the card, a single-use claim code goes on the invitation letter, the member enters it with their phone, the phone is verified by passcode, consent is captured per channel, and the membership is claimed. A reusable code would let anyone holding a discarded letter join.

nodes.label: Product Open Questions
nodes.rationale: Question 1 is recorded as resolved. Still open: priority reservations and event invitations, whether staff record bill amounts, member count and growth, expiry or renewal, who issues invitations, the relationship to H Rewards, platform order, Arabic and English, and the three numbers checked every month.

nodes.label: Three-Phase Delivery
nodes.rationale: Phase 1 core (member app, digital card, claim flow, administrator panel, redemption capture, basic reporting, benefit editing). Phase 2 refinement (tap-to-call, push, fuller reporting, optional wallet pass). Phase 3 if wanted (in-app reservations, event RSVPs, PMS integration).

nodes.label: Steigenberger Doha Privilege Guest Program
nodes.rationale: An existing invitation-only programme extended personally by the Cluster General Manager, with a printed letter, a numbered card (the reference example is PG-0003) and a printed benefits sheet. What does not exist is any digital surface: members cannot look up benefits on a phone and the hotel has no record of who used what.

nodes.label: Single-Use Claim Codes
nodes.rationale: Consumed atomically on first successful activation, at least 128 bits of entropy, never derived from the membership number which is printed on a card and sequential, stored hashed, expiring, bound to one member on issue, with strict rate limiting on the activation endpoint since a guessable claim code grants a genuine membership.

nodes.label: Ten Open Questions
nodes.rationale: The original list the build's Q-numbering derives from, headed by what the existing QR code does, which determines the redemption build. Also asks how many members exist today — the reference card is number three, which is what makes a careful narrow pilot cheap.

nodes.label: Open Questions Q1 to Q11
nodes.rationale: Per build-plan rule 4, a stage that depends on an unanswered question implements the documented assumption, adds a TODO(open-question) comment, and records it here rather than silently deciding. Q2 (bill amounts), Q3 (expiry), Q4 (priority reservations), Q7 (manager write access), Q8 (claim code lifetime) and Q11 (native vs installable) remain open.

nodes.label: Q6 — Passcode Delivery Channel
nodes.rationale: Originally no provider was named anywhere, and the plaintext code was deliberately never logged or returned rather than weakening the control for testing convenience. Closed in Stage 18 by email over SMTP, with the caveat that an administrator must record a member's email at creation time while this is the channel.

nodes.label: Stage 15 — Decisions Before Code
nodes.rationale: Not an engineering task, and it gates the most work per hour of anything in the plan. Q1, Q6 and Q5 actively block Stages 16, 18 and 19; Q11 changes the shape of everything after Stage 17.

nodes.label: Stage 18 — Passcode Delivery
nodes.rationale: No member can sign in without this stage. Build behind a single SmsSender interface so swapping provider later is one file, which matters because the decision may be made on price after a month of real traffic. Qatar specifics with lead times: alphanumeric sender ID registration, delivery to +974 and roaming numbers, and UCS-2 halving the Arabic segment budget.

nodes.label: Product Definition v3
nodes.rationale: Current and authoritative. Version 3 narrows the product after direct client confirmation: exactly two user-facing applications and only named administrators signing in to the hotel panel.

nodes.label: Email-First Passcode Delivery
nodes.rationale: 375 passcodes a month costs under $0.04 by email against $99 by SMS. OTP_DELIVERY_CHANNEL=smtp is already implemented and shipping, so email-first with SMS only for members with no email costs one conditional in the sender and cuts the line by perhaps 80%.

nodes.label: Passcodes Delivered by Email over SMTP
nodes.rationale: The client answered 'Gmail over SMTP'. Gmail cannot send SMS and no email-to-SMS gateway serves +974, so the substance was implemented by treating email as the channel: the phone number stays the identifier and the server looks up the stored address. Explicitly interim and weaker than SMS — whoever controls the mailbox controls the membership.
nodes.norm_label: passcodes delivered by email over smtp

nodes.label: No Points, Tiers or Balances
nodes.rationale: Version 1 assumed a multi-brand coalition with a points currency. All outlets are the hotel's own so there is no settlement between parties; benefits are a fixed discount schedule granted on joining and nothing is earned. If you find yourself writing a balance column, you have misread the specification.

nodes.label: db — postgres:15-alpine (dev)
nodes.rationale: Container pgp-db, published on host port 5433 so it does not collide with a local Postgres. Passwords default to pgp_local_dev / pgp_local_app. The app role created by 01-app-role.sh is deliberately not the owner, so the REVOKE that enforces R7 bites.

nodes.label: Development Compose Stack
nodes.rationale: A development database and nothing else — no API, no edge. The dev and prod files are kept apart so a committed development password can never become a production one.

nodes.label: api Service
nodes.rationale: Built from target 'api', depends_on db with condition service_healthy, joined to both internal and edge networks so Caddy can proxy to it.

nodes.label: db — postgres:16-alpine (prod)
nodes.rationale: No ports section at all: the database is reachable only on the compose network, never from the host or the internet — described as the single most common way a system like this leaks.

nodes.label: edge Network
nodes.rationale: Only Caddy is published; the API joins this network purely so Caddy can proxy to it.

nodes.label: internal Network
nodes.rationale: Marked internal:true — the database and API talk here and it is not routable from outside the host.

nodes.label: Production Compose Stack (pgp)
nodes.rationale: Three services on two networks. Deliberately separate from the development file so no production value has a convenient local default to inherit.

nodes.label: web Service (Caddy Edge)
nodes.rationale: Built from target 'web'. The only published service: 80, 443 and 443/udp for HTTP/3. Certificate volumes survive a rebuild because losing them means re-issuing on every deploy, which Let's Encrypt rate-limits.

nodes.label: Postgres Init Scripts Mount
nodes.rationale: ./docker/postgres/init mounted read-only at /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d, running once on first initialisation of an empty data volume. Mounted identically by both dev and prod.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL 16 Authoritative Store
nodes.rationale: Chosen for exact decimal money, table-level privilege revocation and CHECK constraints. Never exposed to the host or the internet.

nodes.label: Read-Only, No-New-Privileges API Container
nodes.rationale: Nothing is written to disk at runtime; tmpfs covers /tmp so the image itself stays immutable. security_opt no-new-privileges on both api and web.

nodes.label: TRUST_PROXY Behind Caddy
nodes.rationale: X-Forwarded-For is trustworthy behind Caddy. Without this every per-IP rate limit shares one bucket and every audited address is the proxy's — both controls appear present and do nothing.

nodes.label: Two Database URLs, Two Roles
nodes.rationale: DATABASE_URL connects as pgp_app, denied UPDATE and DELETE on Redemption at the database level (R7); DATABASE_MIGRATION_URL connects as pgp_owner. Connecting as the owner would silently remove that guarantee.

nodes.label: Database Role Split (owner vs app)
nodes.rationale: The application connects as a role that is not the schema owner; migrations run as the owner over a separate connection so the revocation cannot be undone by the migration that creates the tables. An owner cannot be denied access to its own tables, so immutability only means something because the application is not the owner.

nodes.label: Redemption Immutability
nodes.rationale: Redemptions cannot be edited or deleted — not by policy but because UPDATE and DELETE are revoked at the database level. A correction is a new reversing row with a negated amount pointing at the original, so totals net correctly without any query knowing about reversals. Idempotency keys stop a retried submission creating a second row.

nodes.label: Eighteen Business Rules
nodes.rationale: R1-R18, each mapped to the stage that enforces it. These are the logic; everything else is plumbing. All eighteen have at least one test by Stage 13.

nodes.label: Things That Will Go Wrong
nodes.rationale: Money as a float, fetch-then-check authorization, 403 for out-of-scope records, hardcoding benefit percentages to move faster, reading alg from the JWT header, adding a staff member search, making redemptions updatable because reversal seemed complicated, logging a member object, and building a points system that does not exist.

nodes.label: R17 — Every Route Declares a Permission
nodes.rationale: An undeclared route fails at startup — the single most important control in the build. The realistic failure is not a broken check but a new endpoint shipped under deadline with no check at all, so forgetting to protect an endpoint becomes a build failure rather than a hole discovered in production.
nodes.norm_label: r17 — every route declares a permission

nodes.label: R18 — Out-of-Scope Records Return 404
nodes.rationale: A 403 confirms the record exists. An out-of-scope record must be byte-identical to a nonexistent one.

nodes.label: Authorization Matrix in CI
nodes.rationale: Administrator and member principals against every endpoint with declared expected outcomes; the build fails on any deviation, and retired database role values are tested as universal denials. Also automated: token manipulation, refresh reuse triggering family revocation, claim code reuse, small-cohort suppression and redemption idempotency under duplicate submission.

nodes.label: Deny by Default, Enforced at Boot
nodes.rationale: Every route declares its required permission and a route with no declaration fails application startup. The single highest-value control: the realistic failure is not a broken check but a new endpoint shipped under deadline with no check at all.
nodes.norm_label: deny by default, enforced at boot

nodes.label: Traps That Do Not Announce Themselves
nodes.rationale: The dangerous class: things that pass every test while being wrong. Spreading a scope fragment, money through a float, a benefit value creeping into code, and 403 where 404 is required.
nodes.norm_label: traps that do not announce themselves

nodes.label: Scope-Spread Clobbering Defect
nodes.rationale: A real defect in the security document's own illustrative snippet. Every lookup returned the caller's own record instead of 404 — a 200 where the answer had to be 404, failing open while looking correct. Fixed with AND composition and pinned by a regression test that demonstrates the old behaviour explicitly.

nodes.label: 403 for a Route, 404 for an Out-of-Scope Record
nodes.rationale: The reasoning for 404 is specifically that a 403 confirms the record exists — it is about records. Which endpoints exist is not a secret (they are in the client bundle), so a 403 on a route leaks nothing.
nodes.norm_label: 403 for a route, 404 for an out-of-scope record

nodes.label: R17 Enforced by an onRoute Hook
nodes.rationale: A registration wrapper only protects routes that remember to use it — a plain app.get() slips straight past, which is precisely the failure the security document describes. Fastify's onRoute hook fires for every route however registered, so there is no bypass to remember.
nodes.norm_label: r17 enforced by an onroute hook

nodes.label: scopedWhere Instead of Spreading the Scope Fragment
nodes.rationale: The security document's illustrative spread is only safe while the fragment shares no keys with the base query. A member's scope is { id: their own id }, so the later spread wins and every lookup returned the caller's own record instead of 404. AND composition cannot clobber.
nodes.norm_label: scopedwhere instead of spreading the scope fragment

nodes.label: Four Principles
nodes.rationale: Fail closed — a missing permission declaration is a denial. Never trust the client — role and scope are resolved server-side on every request. Authorize at the object, not the route: nearly every real-world data leak lives in the gap between confirming a caller is an administrator and confirming the requested record and operation are valid. Minimum exposure.

nodes.label: Scope the Query, Do Not Fetch Then Check
nodes.rationale: Loading a record before authorization is decided leaks its existence through errors, timing and logs. The query must be unable to return a record the caller may not see, and anything out of scope returns 404 rather than 403. Privilege elevation is verified server-side: a client-supplied approved:true is not an authorization decision. The document's own illustrative spread proved unsafe in practice.
nodes.norm_label: scope the query, do not fetch then check
